name: Classical radicalism
summary: Classical radicalism was the leftward wing of liberalism from the late eighteenth to the mid-nineteenth century, centred on Britain. It demanded a far wider franchise, frequent elections and secret ballot, the end of hereditary monarchy, aristocratic privilege and sinecures, freedom of the press, secular or disestablished churches, free trade and cheaper government, and legal and penal reform on rational or utilitarian grounds.
scope: British radicalism c.1780-1870: Paine's Rights of Man, the philosophic radicals (Bentham, James Mill, their circle, with J.S. Mill's liberty doctrine), the Manchester free-traders (Cobden, Bright) and Chartist demands for wider suffrage. Excludes the French Radical Party of 1901 and later socialist or social-liberal radicalism.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Paine
keyFigures.role: Author of Rights of Man, the foundational radical case against hereditary government.

keyFigures.name: Jeremy Bentham
keyFigures.role: Founder of utilitarianism and leading figure of the philosophic radicals.

keyFigures.name: James Mill
keyFigures.role: Bentham's chief disciple, who argued for representative democracy and wider suffrage.

sources.title: Radicals (UK)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Anti-Corn Law League, ballot and suffrage agitation, Chartism, nonconformist and disestablishment demands, slimmed-down executive.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Philosophic radicals drew on Ricardian political economy and the Manchester radicals attacked protection and monopoly, so markets were generally trusted over aristocratic state interference.

public-ownership.rationale: Modern utilities did not exist; radicals distrusted self-interested governments and sought a slimmed-down executive, so large state ownership was not a programme item.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Paine proposed a progressive tax on large estates reaching twenty shillings in the pound at the top, and radicals sought to cut aristocratic privilege, though many mainstream radicals mainly wanted lower taxes overall.

unions-good.rationale: Radicals such as Place campaigned for the right to combine, but philosophic radicals and Manchester liberals were wary of union wage-setting; adherents were split.

property-fundamental.rationale: Radicals defended keeping the fruits of one's labor and Paine counts property among retained rights, but they also attacked feudal landed privilege and primogeniture, so it is not an override-proof right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporations in the modern sense were not the target; radicals opposed monopolies and chartered privilege yet favoured free enterprise, leaving no clear stance.

cut-welfare.rationale: Paine wanted to replace poor-rates with direct grants to the poor, while Benthamites backed the harsh 1834 Poor Law; radicals were mixed, with the humanitarian strand dominating on principle.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Radicals defended a free press and free speech against censorship, and Mill's harm principle rejects restriction for mere offence.

strong-leader.rationale: Radicals sought representative, accountable government with frequent elections and rejected single rulers who could exploit subjects.

state-harmful.rationale: Radicals wanted a reformed, accountable and limited state, not its abolition; Mill called representative government the great modern discovery.

empower-police-military.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and sought cuts in armies and taxation; Paine proposed reducing the army and navy.

decide-locally.rationale: Radicals favoured both wide representative democracy and reform of local corporations; no settled stance on subsidiarity.

rehabilitation.rationale: James Mill's work on prisons treated punishment as remedial education to reform character, and Benthamite penal reform aimed at deterrence and reform rather than cruelty.

traditional-family.rationale: Radicals rejected inherited authority in general and Mill later attacked sex-based subordination, though the family was not a central target.

more-religion-public.rationale: Radicals favoured secularism and anti-clericalism and sought to end church privileges, with Paine insisting religion should not be a state political tool.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Radicalism's civic nationalism and rationalism put reform and universal principles ahead of inherited tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: Radicals sought radical reform of the electoral and legal system and attacked inherited institutions; Paine denied that past generations bind the living.

free-trade.rationale: The Manchester radicals Cobden and Bright led the Anti-Corn Law League against grain duties, and Paine praised commerce as a pacific system that makes nations useful to each other.

nation-first.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and internationalist in outlook, with Paine hoping for peace between nations; mild inference.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Radicals backed liberty abroad but the Manchester wing opposed foreign wars and spending; adherents were split.

revolution-justified.rationale: Paine defended the French revolt against hereditary despotism, while the philosophic radicals worked through lobbying and feared revolutionary excess, so the strands differ.

experts-over-public.rationale: Radicals extended the franchise and held that rulers' interests diverge from the governed, so expertise could not replace democratic accountability; Bentham's technocratic streak makes it mild.

central-planning.rationale: Radical political economy (Ricardo, Mill) and the Manchester men favoured exchange and attacked state-granted privilege.

land-value-tax.rationale: Ricardian rent theory made land taxation attractive to some radicals, but replacing most taxes with it was a later Georgist idea.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Paine's progressive estate tax and abolition of primogeniture aimed to break up large holdings, and radicals attacked inherited privilege.

basic-income.rationale: Paine's grants to children, the old and new mothers resemble it, but unconditional universal income was not proposed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Anti-Corn Law League and the Manchester radicals attacked tariffs as favouring landowners at consumers' expense.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Radicals sought a slimmed-down executive and opposed state-granted privilege and monopoly.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Paine's tax scheme and attack on primogeniture were designed to divide large estates, and radicals sought wider property ownership against aristocratic land concentration.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not a classical radical aim; the tradition accepted market exchange and wages.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Banking policy was debated among radicals (Cobbett attacked paper money) but not as an agreed position.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised bodies setting wages are contrary to liberal-radical individualism and political economy.

one-party-rule.rationale: Radicals demanded wide suffrage, frequent elections and free press; single-party rule contradicts representative government.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Paine condemned hereditary monarchy as despotism, James Mill rejected monarchy as exploitable, and republicanism is listed among radical positions.

democracy-best.rationale: Radicals favoured democratic accountability, though James Mill and Bentham worried about interest and J.S. Mill later weighted votes; the core is pro-democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: Direct democracy is listed among radical associations, but the philosophic radicals prized representative government as the grand modern discovery; split.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils replacing parliaments are alien to a tradition that built on parliamentary reform and wider suffrage.

natural-rulers.rationale: Paine said all men are born equal with equal natural right and condemned hereditary government; Mill rejected ruling elites.

political-violence-never.rationale: Philosophic radicals avoided violence and feared revolutionary excess, whereas Paine and Chartists accepted force in extremity; mostly not an absolute rule.

war-builds-character.rationale: Paine wrote he wished war might never exist, and radicals were antimilitarist.

separate-church-state.rationale: Secularism, anti-clericalism and disestablishment were radical causes, and Paine treated religion as a private right.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Rationalism and secularism led radicals to ground law in utility and reason; Paine and Bentham attacked religious authority over government.

military-superiority.rationale: Antimilitarism and calls for reduced armies and navies, and for lower taxes, were radical themes.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Radical nationalism was civic, and Paine's principles rest on equal rights of all men.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Radicals saw conflict between rulers and ruled, aristocracy versus people, but not Marxist class struggle as history's motor; Chartists were more class-conscious.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Radicals added equality to liberal rights, but of rights and opportunity and ending privilege, not equal outcomes; Paine's grants were minimal relief.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Bentham and James Mill held that people pursue their own pleasure and designed institutions around it; calling it morally good is more utilitarian than selfish, and J.S. Mill rejected the egoism.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Radicals started from natural and equal individual rights, as in Paine.

limit-population.rationale: Malthusian ideas split radicals: Place promoted birth control, while Paine-style and Cobbett views differed.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Radicals welcomed commerce and industry, with free-trade manufacturers (the Manchester men) at the forefront.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Radicals favoured progress but also gradual legislation and did not endorse disruption for its own sake.

restore-past-order.rationale: Radicals attacked inherited institutions; Paine rejected governing from the grave and prized the present generation's authority.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Utilitarian philosophic radicals judged institutions by their consequences for happiness, a strongly results-oriented outlook.

direct-action.rationale: Philosophic radicals worked through lobbying and parliament; the Chartist mass demonstrations also petitioned parliament, though some wings used physical force.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Contrary to the commerce and progress orientation of the tradition.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Ricardian political economy accepted specialisation and exchange.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Classical radicals thought people should keep the fruits of their labor; Paine's grants were targeted relief.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Radicals attacked aristocratic and rentier privilege more than industrial profit, and Ricardian economics did not treat profit as exploitation; some labour radicals differed.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Incompatible with the radical demand for wide suffrage and representative accountability.

collective-farming.rationale: Radicals aimed at dividing landed estates among many owners, not collectivisation.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Cobden and Bright argued commerce promotes peace and Paine called it pacific, which is the opposite thesis; but critics of empire among radicals also blamed arms and aristocracy.

taxation-theft.rationale: Radicals accepted taxation, wanting it lower and fairer, and Paine proposed tax-funded relief.

harm-principle.rationale: J.S. Mill's harm principle is the classic statement within the tradition, though earlier radicals such as Bentham reasoned from utility instead.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Radicals championed individual rights, but groups such as nonconformists and women received claims and Bentham called natural rights nonsense; split.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Radicals made the vote the central check, with frequent elections to align rulers' interests with the people's.

state-as-business.rationale: Radicals sought accountable government of the people, not customer-service governance.

positive-liberty.rationale: Radicalism added social and educational reform to liberal rights, but positive-liberty theory is later; Mill's education stress points mildly toward it.

media-academia-power.rationale: Radicals regarded the press as a check on rulers, but not as the true power over elected officials.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Radicals held that character is formed by circumstances and that all men are equal; racial hierarchy was contrary to Paine's principles.

organic-representation.rationale: Radicals favoured representation of individuals by equal suffrage, against corporate and hereditary bodies.

national-rebirth.rationale: Radicals sought reform of institutions via reason, not mythic national regeneration.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Antimilitarism and the Manchester opposition to costly foreign adventures.

bound-labor.rationale: Paine's principle that no generation or man has property in man; radicals attacked feudal privilege and backed anti-slavery.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Rationalism and Enlightenment confidence in reason as the guide to truth.

universal-morality.rationale: Radicals relied on reason and universal principles (equal natural rights, utility), with J.S. Mill adding qualifications.

single-common-good.rationale: Utilitarians aimed at the greatest happiness, but also argued rulers' interests diverge from the governed and so built institutions to balance interests; split.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Democratic accountability was a political principle; workplace extension was a later (Mill's cooperatives, Owenite) idea not shared by the mainstream.

rule-by-example.rationale: Radicals relied on laws, institutions and accountability rather than rulers' virtue, assuming rulers pursue self-interest.

national-self-determination.rationale: Civic nationalism and support for liberal revolutions such as Belgium's and the 1848 uprisings.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Rationalism is a defining radical trait, and Paine's Rights of Man names reason as the only legitimate source of government against superstition and power.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Radicals never debated limiting welfare by citizenship; Paine's relief scheme was framed for the poor generally.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Benthamite poor-law reformers favoured work conditions, while Paine's grants were unconditional except schooling; split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Middle-class radicals stressed shared interest against landlords, while working-class radicals saw conflict; split.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: James Mill excluded women from the vote on the basis of household interest, but Thompson and J.S. Mill criticised it; on balance reformers moved toward equality.

ban-interest.rationale: Political economy of Bentham (his defence of usury) and Ricardo favoured free lending.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Radicals argued that rulers use government for their own interests, which resembles this, but no class theory; split by wording.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy claim foreign to rationalist radicalism.

proportional-representation.rationale: J.S. Mill backed proportional representation (Hare), but most radicals sought equal districts and the ballot; split.

national-mission.rationale: Radicals backed liberal revolutions but opposed costly interventions, with Paine hoping republics would spread by example.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Mill's later writings point to yes and Thompson's Appeal attacked women's exclusion, but the early philosophic radicals denied it.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Radicalism arose against rotten boroughs, sinecures and aristocratic misrule, and Bentham and Mill held rulers pursue their own interest.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Contrary to equal rights and the harm principle.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Manchester radicals sought a slimmed state, while Benthamites favoured active legal and administrative reform; split.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Paine states that all men are born equal with equal natural right, and radicals pressed for equality before the law.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Radicals sought equal rights regardless of religion, including admission of nonconformists to office.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Paine treated religion as a retained natural right, and radicals sought toleration and freedom of conscience.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Religious prohibitions imposed by law conflict with secular utilitarian reasoning.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Paine holds that legitimate government rests on the people and that government is for the living.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Free-trade radicals prized competition, but did not make struggle between peoples the engine of progress; split.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Radicals opposed aggressive war, but accepted state coercion through taxes and law.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Paine's attack on hereditary power, called slavery, and radical concern with rulers' arbitrary power match it.

separated-powers.rationale: Paine defended constitutions as limits on government, while philosophic radicals chiefly relied on accountable legislature; mild.

vanguard-party.rationale: Foreign to a tradition built on mass reform movements and parliamentary pressure.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Paine's tax-funded relief for the poor, and radical attacks on privilege, point to yes; Manchester strand less so.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Place and radicals fought combination laws, but political economists doubted union effects.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusians such as James Mill and Ricardo's circle accepted it, but Paine and Cobbett blamed institutions; split.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Radicals sought toleration of nonconformists and civic nationalism.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Radicals relied on elections to align interests; lottery was not a program.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Radicals fought repression of press and assembly, and trusted no ruler with unchecked power.

party-controls-media.rationale: Radicals defended freedom of the press against censorship.

party-commands-army.rationale: Contrary to accountable constitutional government and antimilitarism.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Radicals prized independent representatives accountable to voters, not party discipline.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Radicals rejected hereditary or executive prerogative, wanting the legislature to control government.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Anti-clerical and disestablishmentarian radicals opposed privileged episcopal establishment.

clerical-rule.rationale: Radicals campaigned against the established church's political privileges and for secular government (s1), which rules out clergy holding supreme power.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Radicals opposed war, but wishing defeat is a Leninist formula.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Radicals defended free press and free expression; Mill rejects moralistic restriction.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Radicals wanted frequent elections and short terms to align interests.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Contrary to property and market outlook.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Cobbett idealised rural life, whereas manufacturing radicals championed towns; split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: No stated radical position on reunifying divided nations; consent and self-determination give only weak guidance.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Radicals prized education and reason; hostility to educated classes was not a theme.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Radicals held universal rational standards, but opposed hierarchy of peoples; split.

death-penalty.rationale: Benthamite penal reform emphasised reform and proportion, tending toward limiting capital punishment; gravest-crime exceptions were accepted by some.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Rationalism and secularism oppose religious dogma in schooling.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: J.S. Mill valued a large variety of characters and lifestyles and tied liberty to individuality.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Not a classical radical theme; the tradition sought political and legal reform rather than economic transformation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Paine defines a constitution as antecedent to government and made by the people.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Radical political liberty (press, suffrage) was not traded for other ends.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Republicanism and consent doctrine favour an elected head over hereditary or indirect selection.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Utilitarians justify property by utility, while Paine and Mill treat it as protected; split on wording.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Radicals were republicans, rejecting a symbolic hereditary head.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Consent doctrine and antimilitarism point against force.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Paine attacks hereditary monarchy and the claim of divine origin for kings in Rights of Man (s4), which directly rejects a sacred ruler; he does not discuss divine descent in those words.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Paine's progressive scheme opposes flat rates, though income tax itself was not mainstream.

character-from-environment.rationale: Mill called education the means of forming character, and J.S. Mill stressed circumstances and education in shaping character, central to the Benthamite reform programme.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Radicals demanded accountable rulers and Paine insisted government is a creature of a constitution.

mixed-constitution.rationale: James Mill rejected aristocracy and monarchy and favoured representation by the many.

land-redistribution.rationale: Paine aimed at dividing estates by taxation and abolishing primogeniture, but seizure and redistribution was only the Spencean fringe; split.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Contrary to consent doctrine and civic nationalism.

worker-ownership.rationale: Collective worker ownership was an Owenite and later idea; classical radicals sought wider individual property and market enterprise, with only J.S. Mill later sympathetic to cooperatives.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Radicals wanted a limited, accountable state and cheaper government; strengthening state power for security runs against that.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Political economists of the radical circle (Ricardo, Mill) and Manchester free-traders opposed fixing prices, though radicals protested grain-price distress.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Radicals attacked aristocracy, sinecures and hereditary privilege; abolition of titles is among the positions listed for radicalism.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Radicals wanted sovereignty in a wide electorate and distrusted aristocratic institutions, but the Mills and Paine also stressed rights and the danger of majority tyranny; adherents split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Radicals, especially the Manchester free-traders, campaigned against the Corn Laws and for open trade and cheap government.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Radicals mainly sought reform by agitation, petition and the vote; the Chartist physical-force wing was a minority, so the idea is mostly rejected.

public-money-creation.rationale: Chartist and Attwoodite currency reformers wanted public control of money while the Philosophic Radicals and Paine distrusted paper issues; adherents split.

delink-world-market.rationale: Free trade was a core radical demand, notably the Anti-Corn Law League, so cutting ties with the world market runs against it.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Paine championed written constitutions that bind government, but Bentham and the utilitarians rejected natural rights as a basis, so adherents were divided.

elective-rulers.rationale: Radicals, following Paine, rejected hereditary monarchy and aristocracy and wanted government by election.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Paine argued that governments rest on consent and may be changed when they break trust.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The radical programme sought a wide franchise and an elected legislature as the seat of authority.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Radicals held relief as a right and attacked aristocratic privilege, not paternal duty.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Radicals campaigned for franchise, reform and public activity.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Free-trade radicals favoured open commerce over self-reliance.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Radicals were antimilitarist and opposed standing armies and military power over civil government.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Radicals wanted frequent elections but not instructed delegates; Mill defended representatives' independent judgment.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Split: Paine proposed tax-funded old-age support while Manchester radicals preferred self-help and thrift.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Mainstream radicals defended private property, though Mill and some radicals backed land reform against aristocratic landed estates.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Radicals demanded cheap, accountable government and Commons control of taxation and spending against the Crown and aristocracy.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Cobden and Bright opposed foreign entanglements and armed intervention, though many radicals sympathised with foreign liberal movements.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Cobden and Bright championed non-intervention in other states' affairs and opposed military force abroad.

democratic-peace.rationale: Paine argued that representative republics would end the wars of kings, and Cobden and Bright tied free government and trade to peace.

non-intervention.rationale: Cobden and Bright's Manchester radicals opposed foreign interventions and standing armaments, though radicals were not uniform on this.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Bentham and the philosophic radicals made publicity of government a safeguard against misrule, alongside freedom of the press.

local-production.rationale: The programme included free trade and cheaper government, which sits against a preference for mainly local production.

religious-nation.rationale: Radicals demanded secular or disestablished churches and religious equality, which excludes defining the nation by religion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Paine and the Manchester free-traders saw commerce and industry as engines of progress and peace, a view documented in the radical tradition.

socialized-care.rationale: Domestic work as a public service is a later socialist idea; radicals favoured limited, cheap government and private family arrangements.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Owenite communities were a separate socialist current; mainstream radicals stressed individual rights, property and national representation.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Radicals demanded freedom of the press and free expression, as in Paine's Rights of Man and Mill's liberty doctrine.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Radicals wanted secular or disestablished churches and, in Mill's doctrine, no punishment of opinions.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Free-trade radicals such as Cobden and Bright opposed colonial expansion as costly and aristocratic.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Paine in Rights of Man holds that sovereignty resides in the nation and rejects government by divine right or hereditary claim.

social-market-economy.rationale: They favoured free trade and cheap government and so opposed state-run economies, though some accepted limited reform.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: They wanted cheaper government and smaller standing armies but did not call for abolition.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Cobden and Bright championed non-intervention and opposed entanglement in great-power alliances and wars.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Paine's Rights of Man attacks hereditary government as a usurpation of the rights of later generations, and radicals demanded an end to hereditary monarchy.

property-franchise.rationale: Early radicals demanded broad or universal male suffrage, as Paine and the Chartists did, though some philosophic radicals like James Mill accepted limits; a minority position among them.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Radicals campaigned for a free, cheap press against stamp taxes and noted the influence of wealth and aristocracy, though they largely thought liberty enough, so mild agree.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Paine and Bentham demanded government by known, public laws against arbitrary rule and sinecure; legal reform and codification were central radical goals.

open-government-data.rationale: Bentham's publicity principle held that open government is a check on misrule, and radicals attacked secrecy and corruption in government.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Radicals favoured disestablishment, religious toleration and civil marriage for dissenters; they opposed legal religious restrictions.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Classical radicals demanded toleration and equal civil rights regardless of religion, as in the Mill liberty doctrine; targeting a minority conflicts with that.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Radicals were rationalist and anti-clerical, attacking established churches and urging that belief be tested by reason, as in Paine; they favoured rethinking inherited doctrine.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Paine proposed progressive taxes on large estates to curb aristocratic accumulation and the radicals attacked aristocratic privilege, but they accepted private property broadly.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Radicals sought secular or disestablished churches and freedom of conscience, not state promotion of unbelief; Paine was a deist and defended liberty of conscience.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Radicals reformed rather than abolished the penal system; Bentham designed prisons and the radicals sought rational penal reform.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Paine proposed state-funded poor relief and the radicals sought to replace aristocratic patronage with rational public provision, so they did not rely on charity.

term-limits.rationale: Radicals demanded frequent elections and an end to sinecures and career placemen; Paine and the Chartists urged annual parliaments, close to limits on tenure though not term limits as such.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: J.S. Mill's circle later argued marital equality, but James Mill and most radicals did not; split.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Nuclear weapons postdate the movement; its general anti-militarism points slightly one way but adherents cannot be placed, so this is neutral.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Radicals attacked sinecures, aristocratic privilege and unearned rents, and Mill criticised income from mere ownership of land.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Most utilitarian and liberal radicals accepted force in self-defence; only a Quaker-influenced minority held absolute non-killing.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Rationalist and utilitarian radicals disliked glorifying death for the nation as military and aristocratic sentiment, and sacralising it more so.

culture-before-state.rationale: Radicals focused on reforming government and the state first (franchise, ballot, legal reform) rather than a cultural renewal.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Mill later wrote for women's equality, but radicals as a whole took no common line on judging scripture.

second-chamber.rationale: Radicals attacked the hereditary House of Lords and aristocratic privilege, so a second chamber was suspect.

person-over-state.rationale: Mill's liberty doctrine and Paine's rights of man make the individual's rights prior to state ends.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Cobden and Bright championed peace, non-intervention and cheaper government, opposing aggressive wars.

arms-reduction.rationale: Radicals demanded cheap government and opposed standing armies and military expenditure; Cobden and Bright campaigned for retrenchment and peace.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Radicals attacked secret diplomacy as aristocratic; Cobden and Bright demanded open foreign policy and publicity.

capital-controls.rationale: Radicals championed free trade and free commerce; Cobden and the Manchester school opposed state interference with trade and capital.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Radicals were split: they favoured citizen militias over standing armies, but also backed order against mobs, and the sources opened do not settle this.

sacred-nation.rationale: Radicals were rationalist and cosmopolitan; Paine's Rights of Man rejects mystic inherited authority and treats the nation as a society of equal citizens.

workers-own-party.rationale: Radicals led parliamentary reform, and Chartists demanded a wider franchise rather than a class party, so the demand for a separate workers' party is not one this mainstream held.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: The radicals attacked hereditary and aristocratic privilege and demanded representation by elected government, so a formal role for traditional leaders is the opposite of their programme.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Penal reform on rational or utilitarian grounds, as Bentham argued, favoured calibrating punishment to the case and cutting excessive fixed penalties like capital offences.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Radicals sought disestablishment and an end to the privileges of the established church.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Radicals centred reform on frequent, competitive elections and the secret ballot, though J.S. Mill also worried about majority tyranny; adherents leaned procedural.

premarital-sex.rationale: Adherents were split: Bentham and Mill were permissive on sexual morality, but Victorian moral reformers also sat among the radicals.

women-suffrage.rationale: J.S. Mill and Bentham argued for votes for women, though James Mill disagreed, so the radical mainstream was split but leaned in favor.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Adherents were split: Lockean-leaning radicals accepted ownership by labour, while Paine treated the earth as common property.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Radicals championed free trade, cheap government and a slimmed-down executive, opposed to state-run planned economies.

indirect-election.rationale: They demanded a wide direct franchise, the secret ballot and frequent elections, not election by intermediate bodies.

national-church-status.rationale: Disestablishment of the Church of England and equality of religious bodies were central radical and nonconformist demands.

self-ownership.rationale: J.S. Mill's liberty doctrine and the radical emphasis on equal natural rights supports personal sovereignty over body and labour.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The Anti-Corn Law League attacked taxes on bread and other food and radicals demanded cheaper government and lower taxation.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Radicals demanded a wider franchise and representative government; they sought to empower parties and the electorate, not a leader outside them, and rejected hereditary rule.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Radicals attacked sinecures, aristocratic privilege and monopolies, and the Corn Laws as a landowner privilege.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Disestablishment of churches and secularism were radical aims, which opposes denominationally organised politics.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The philosophic radicals followed Bentham and James Mill's utilitarianism, which rejects natural law; law was judged by its consequences, though Paine's natural rights stood opposed.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Paine wanted to replace poor-rates with direct grants to the poor, while Benthamites backed the harsh 1834 Poor Law; radicals were mixed, with the humanitarian strand dominating on principle. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Seats in the legislature should be filled by a wide franchise of ordinary citizens, not limited to property owners.
missingStatements.rationale: Extension of the franchise was the defining radical demand, argued by Bentham, the Mills and the Chartists.

missingStatements.text: Voting should be by secret ballot.
missingStatements.rationale: James Mill's 1830 essay The Ballot defended secret voting as protection against intimidation, and radical pressure led to the Ballot Act 1872.
missingStatements.declined: Settled in every modern democracy; no ideology in the bank would take the opposite side, so it fails the contested test.

missingStatements.text: Hereditary titles and privileges should be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: Radicals attacked aristocracy, sinecures and hereditary privilege; abolition of titles is among the positions listed for radicalism.

notes: Strands differ: Paine and Chartists were more egalitarian and sympathetic to force, philosophic radicals were utilitarian and constitutional, and Manchester radicals prioritised free trade and cheap government. Several answers are split for that reason. Statement ids with no period analogue are low-confidence inferences.
